senses: To vary irregularly; to swing.
To undulate.
To be irresolute; to waver.
To cause to vary irregularly.
ety: First attested in 1630; borrowed from Latin flūctuātus, perfect passive participle of flūctuō (“(of the sea) to surge, swell; (of man) to waver, fluctuate”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix).
examples: One of them, at great Expence of Algebra, proves, that the Motes, which in Scotomias, we seem to have in our Eyes, are not real Bodies fluctuating in them.
I fluctuated between wishing he was back home and wishing I'd never met him.

senses: A rampart or other defensive entrenchment that entirely encircles the position being defended.
ety: Borrowed from Latin circumvāllātiō. By surface analysis, circumvallate + -ation.
examples: The Saxon architect had exhausted his art in rendering the main keep defensible, and there was no other circumvallation than a rude barrier of palisades.
He just managed to finish her in time—the day before the date fixed for his breaking ground on a greater business still, the circumvallation of Mrs. Dunn.

senses: The keystone of an arch.
A metal wedge which fits into the space between the type and the edge of a chase, and is tightened to fix the metal type in place.
A number of apple varieties with a distinctive ribbed appearance, like corners of a coin.
ety: Variant of coin; compare coign.
examples: Next fit the quoins, using the “persuader” to squeeze in the pages, and tap up all around.

senses: A creature or creatures from hell.
Any monster; a vicious fiend or villain.
ety: From hell + spawn.
examples: Despite his grim mien, his kinship with vein-biters and hellspawns, Batman always maintained one pious virtue, his unspoken insistence on the value—the sacredness—of human life.
Image Animation also fabricated the hellspawns’ bondage-inspired costumes, substituting foam material for the more expensive leather of the previous two films.
The face and voice were beyond question those of the man who had died to protect her in a room full of hellspawn and slaughter.

senses: A series of related items.
A series of distinct soils arrayed along a slope.
ety: From Medieval Latin catena, from Latin catēna (“chain”). Doublet of chain.
examples: The changes in soil characteristics from the crest to the foot of a slope are together known as a catena.

senses: A noisy party or festivities.
A noisy argument.
ety: Origin uncertain; perhaps an alteration of shindy, or from Scottish Gaelic sìnteag (“jump, leap”).
examples: They'd get up a regular shindig, if it wasn't for making too much noise.
There was bound to be a New Year's shindig going on in his apartment down on Las Palmas.

senses: Fraught with angst.
Insecure and moody or thorny.
ety: From angst + -y.
examples: Jackson said industrial relations felt "angsty" at a national level.

senses: Repulsive, inspiring aversion.
Resistant or impervious to something.
ety: From Latin repellēns. Equivalent to repel + -ent.
examples: The mixture of whey, beetroot juice, and spirulina seems repellent to me.
All that fabric's supposed to be dust-repellent.

senses: to remove excess blood from by washing and salting
to remove traces of non-kosher substances from by cleaning, heating, etc.
ety: Borrowed from Yiddish כּשרן (kashern), from כּשר (kosher, “kosher”).
examples: David moved into his new apartment, put up mezuzahs, and kashered his new kitchen.

senses: worthless; unpleasant
Dirty with feces.
Resembling or characteristic of feces.
needing to poop (defecate)
ety: From poop + -y. Compare shitty.
examples: You don't throw a six-year-old into a sandbox and say: "Hey! You can only make poopy castles!" You know when you take wet sand and just let it drip on top of a pile of sand? It's a poopy castle.
Can we stop the car? I'm poopy.

senses: Death, such as from heart attack or stroke, brought on by overwork or job-related stress.
ety: Borrowed from Japanese 過労死 (karōshi), from 過労 (karō, “overwork”) + 死 (shi, “death”). Doublet of guolaosi and gwarosa.
examples: For a while he began to speak Japanese, rather slangy, never having seemed to learn it — karoshi for death from overwork, yakitaori-ya for eatery, and gaijin for clumsy foreigner.
Second, we discuss the problem of karoshi, which is unique to Japan. Karoshi has become an increasingly serious problem.
Since the 1980s, labor lawyers and citizens groups have been pushing for changes to the law to recognize karoshi as a serious social issue.

senses: One who tames or subdues.
ety: From tame (verb) + -er (suffix forming agent nouns).
examples: Only Enid could dare him at such a time, and even she felt occasionally that sinking of the heart which the bravest of tamers may experience as he unbars the gate of the cage.
On the mantelshelf either side of the clock stood two lacquered bronzes of horse and tamer.
You came back from that island alive! Mate, yeer a bloomin' freak of nature! Yer a master! Yer a true tamer of the high seas! Yer more man than I am!

senses: A tempo mark directing that a passage is to be played at an increasing speed.
A passage having this mark.
Accelerating or exponential advancement or development (of a thing).
ety: Borrowed from Italian accelerando, from Latin accelero.
examples: The accelerando of the sciences and of technology, their mathematization have beggared both the reach and the veracity of natural language.

senses: The property of being directionally dependent.
The degree to which this property is exhibited.
ety: From an- + isotropy.
examples: Velvet exhibits anisotropy when rotated about its geometric normal.

senses: A traditional shallow, two-handled cup of Scottish origin symbolizing friendship, originally used to toast the arrival or departure of a visitor.
Any two-handled drinking vessel or trophy.
ety: From Scots quaich, from Scottish Gaelic cuach (“bowl, goblet”), from Old Irish cuäch (“goblet”), from Proto-Celtic *kaɸukos (“cup, bowl, vessel”).
examples: Every evening through all the summer Lampusa put out for them before her rock-hewn kitchen a silver quaich of milk; then she summoned the creatures with a low call.

senses: Similar to, or tasting like beef.
Containing beef.
Strong or muscular.
Large; overweight; fat.
Sturdy; robust.
ety: From beef + -y.
examples: The Chicken Big Mac is similar to its beefy sibling; however, it replaces the two burgers with two tempura chicken patties.
The barman was a big, beefy guy with his sleeves rolled up and tattoos on his arms.
The jaw bone in particular “looks more like that of H. erectus … than the beefier jaws of more primitive hominins such as H. habilis,” according to science journal Nature.

senses: The transformation of something into a commodity.
ety: From commoditize + -ation.
examples: The gay capitalists are identifying the commoditization of homosexuality with liberation.
Having established this ultimate, farcical commoditization of heroism, Robbins turns his attention to Carlos.

senses: To safeguard or protect something as if by inoculation.
To add one substance to another.
To graft by inserting buds.
To introduce into the mind (used especially of harmful ideas or principles).
ety: First attested in c. 1440; inherited from Middle English inoculaten (“to graft”), from Latin inoculātus, perfect passive participle of inoculō (“to ingraft an eye or bud of one plant into (another), implant”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from in- (“in”) + oculus (“an eye”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix).
examples: Her upbringing overseas inoculated her against prejudice.
The culture medium was inoculated with selenium to investigate the rate of uptake.
And in Aprill figtreen inoculate

senses: A person who practises or studies occultism; a practitioner of, or person learned in, the occult.
ety: From occult + -ist.
examples: Albertus Magnus, the thirteenth century philosopher and occultist, states that coriander, valerian, and violet are love producing herbs.

In the early 1930s, he fell under the spell of a wife-beating, alcoholic, Austrian occultist called Karl Maria Wiligut and a Dutch prehistorian called Herman Wirth, whose views further fed his fantastical illusions.

senses: A fortification or barrier such as a small earthen mound or ridge, a file of troops, etc.
ety: Borrowed from French rideau (“curtain”), from Middle French rideau, from Old French ridel (“plaited stuff; cloth curtain; blind”), from rider (“to plait; to wrinkle”), perhaps from Old High German ridil (“a headband; a ribbon”) or rīdan, wrīdan (“to wrinkle”) (related to English writhe), from Proto-Germanic *wriþilaz, from *wrīþaną (“to twist, wind, wrap”). See more at riddle (“curtain”), writhe.
examples: About the 24th proposal was made for taking the enemy's vessels, three of which were at anchor a little below the fort, and some of their rideaus likewise.

senses: Becoming putrid; putrefying.
ety: Attested since circa 1730, from Latin pūtrēscēns (“rotting”), present participle of pūtrēscō (“rot”).
examples: When it is combined with that quantity of water with which it is found united in the gall-bladder, it is not more putrescent than the serum of the blood

This same reason accounts to a considerable extent for the fact, that soft steeping liquor, if seldom changed, becomes much more putrescent than hard water retained with the same barleys for a similar period in cistern.

senses: To give a dower or dowry to.
ety: From Middle English dower, dowere, from Old French doeire, from Medieval Latin dōtārium, from Latin dōs. Doublet of dowry.
examples: He had married a lady well educated and softly nurtured, but not dowered with worldly wealth.

senses: Shabbat or shabbat (the biblical seventh-day Sabbath).
ety: Borrowed from Yiddish שבת (shabes), from Hebrew שַׁבָּת (shabát). Doublet of Shabbat and Sabbath.
examples: I told that Kraut a fuckin' thousand times, I don't roll on shabbos!
Many of the housemates had Jewish ancestry, but in lieu of Shabbos prayers they had invented their own secular rituals.

senses: Having prominent lips.
Having a tendency to talk back in a cheeky or impertinent manner.
ety: From lip (“fleshy protrusion around the opening of the mouth; (slang) verbal impertinence, backtalk”) + -y (suffix forming adjectives with the sense of ‘having the quality of’).
examples: His eyes were large and prominent, his mouth wide and lippy, and as he bent over his books he emitted sundry low growls and grunts, plainly indicating that his temper was none of the sweetest.
Don't give me any lip! I don't like how lippy you've been acting lately! Clean your room.
I hesitated another moment, then followed her with a vow that I would walk out the instant she got lippy. If she wanted to fire me, fine, I'd go, but I'd be damned if I'd let her lay any crap on me.

senses: Having a dank quality resulting from excessive ageing in a tank.
Able to withstand much damage, having a lot of hit points (that is, like a tank).
ety: From tank + -y (adjectival suffix).
examples: When it comes to weakside tanks, Sion is the tankiest of the bunch. Between Heartsteel and his max HP stacking on W, killing Sion takes forever.
The demon lord that is Mauga has been a top-tier option since Season 11’s midseason patch, and he’s still tankier than ever in Season 13.
If the added physical damage to enemies wasn’t enough, Qionjiu can also apply Burn damage which helps chew through tanky enemies.

senses: In Arab contexts: a catastrophe; a grave setback.
ety: Borrowed from Arabic نَكْبَة (nakba, “disaster, catastrophe”); see further at Nakba.
examples: Our President is admitting that the war has been a nakba, a setback. 'I take full personal responsibility.' 'But not for long,' murmurs Mahmoud, in whose company I am watching this ultra-dramatic moment.
A second nakba happened after the 1967 Six Day War, when Israel captured Arab land that belonged to Jordan and Egypt; another 325,000 Palestinians left their homes.
But for now, there is no prophet amongst the politicians, and the only prophecies to be heard are of nakbas and holocausts.

senses: A web page, usually carrying advertising, displayed when leaving one content page for another.
ety: From Latin interstitiālis. By surface analysis, interstitium + -al.
examples: An interstitial appeared before the download.
Interstitials should be used sparingly. Display an ad only the first time the user accesses a piece of content, not every time.

senses: To survive on a minimum of resources.
To have ontological reality; to exist.
To retain a certain state; to continue.
ety: From Latin subsistō (“halt, stop”), from sub (“below”) + sistō (“stand, place”). Compare consist, desist, exist, insist, persist.
examples: Subject to section 5(1), copyright subsists only by virtue of this Act.

If there is a choice between improving the lot of the poor but allowing inequality to subsist, or leaving the poor as they are and depressing everyone to their level, it is the second alternative that must be chosen.

senses: Causing privation; depriving.
Consisting in the absence of something; negative.
ety: From Latin privativus.
examples: Privative blessings, blessings of immunity, safeguard, liberty, and integrity.

senses: A set of spiritual practices and traditions created and concealed from slave-owners by enslaved Africans in North America, based on traditional African beliefs.
A practitioner of voodoo.
Supernatural bad luck, or something or someone believed to bring bad luck.
ety: Apparently an alteration of voodoo.
examples: The three men wondered whether they would find Colson at Taylor's Creek. They felt that a hoodoo hung over the place.

senses: A combat engineer; an engineer or a soldier engaged in attacking, destroying, and circumventing or building fortifications, bridges, and roads; a military engineer active in a combat zone.
An officer or private of the Royal Engineers.
a person generally engaged in digging requiring a level of professionalism
ety: Borrowed from Middle French sappeur (French sapeur). By surface analysis, sap + -er.
examples: A vast minefield trapped Ukrainian troops for weeks as infantry sappers slowly cleared an assault route on foot.

Billinge, from St Austell, was one of the first soldiers to land on 'Gold' beach on June 6 1944. He was a sapper attached to the 44 Royal Engineer Commandos and was one of only four to survive from his unit.
Let no Bank consider itself safe from the skill and daring of such sappers and miners.

senses: A vacation spent at or close to home.
A vacation spent at one's own home without other overnight accommodation.
ety: The noun is a blend of stay (at home) + vacation. The verb is derived from the noun.
examples: If you're feeling the pinch of high gas prices and job woes, try a "Staycation", the new industry term for staying at home and enjoying yourself.

Instead of going away for a vacation, consider a staycation. That's when you stay home and explore your hometown—try a new restaurant, hike a local park, or visit that museum you've been meaning to check out.
I could stop this right now, I thought. We could unpack the car and go back to our lives—a staycation in our own home.

senses: the act of oscillating or the state of being oscillated
a regular periodic fluctuation in value about some mean
a single such cycle
ety: From French oscillation, from Latin oscillatio, from Latin oscillo. By surface analysis, oscillate + -ion.
examples: The trial running tests which were made with the vehicles showed that they ride very steadily laterally, with almost complete absence of oscillation at all speeds.

senses: To cause nausea in.
To become squeamish; to feel nausea; to turn away with disgust.
ety: From earlier nauseat, from Latin nauseātus (“nauseated”), perfect past participle of nauseō (“to feel sea sick, nauseate”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix, of participial origin)), from nausea, from Ancient Greek ναυσία (nausía), from ναῦς (naûs), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)neh₂-. By surface analysis, nausea + -ate (verb-forming suffix).
examples: After another three-quarters of an hour we pick up eleven children, nearly all of them objectionable on the score of smell. The air we breathe over and over begins to be so foul that it nauseates me.
As one of Woodward’s Patients, sick and sore, I puke, I nauseate,—yet he thrusts in more;
I prescribed Iodized Lime, 1-2 grain every half hour. The stomach soon began to nauseate.

senses: A type of instrumental suite popular in the 18th century
ety: From Italian partita. Doublet of party and partie.
examples: He starts with scales and arpeggios, then something more substantial, on a recent day one of Bach’s partitas for the violin.

senses: Offering nothing that is stimulating or challenging.
Lifeless, dull, or banal.
Tasteless, bland, or insipid.
ety: Borrowed from Latin vapidus (“flat, vapid”).
examples: Then there was a little more trite conversation between Mr. Arabin and Mr. Harding; trite, and hard, and vapid, and senseless.

senses: A transparent olive green form of olivine, used as a gem.
A yellow-green color, like that of the peridot.
ety: From Middle English peritot, from Anglo-Norman peridou, peridout, Middle French perido, peridon, of uncertain origin; later reborrowed from modern French péridot.
examples: Gem-quality olivine is known as peridot, which has a subtle green light all its own.

senses: Resembling or characteristic of influenza.
ety: From flu + -like.
examples: The patient presented with flulike symptoms.

senses: A Jewish folk musician.
A type of popular Jewish folk music especially associated with Ashkenazi cultures.
ety: Borrowed from Yiddish קלעזמער (klezmer), from Hebrew כְּלֵי זֶמֶר (kléy zémer, “musical instruments”).
examples: The entire Muzikant family of klezmorim, enough for half a symphony orchestra.

senses: A drink made of wine, often port, mixed with hot water, oranges or lemons, spices and sugar.
ety: Named after Colonel Francis Negus (1670–1732), its creator.
examples: And when he got home he had a glass of hot negus in his wife's sitting-room, and read the last number of the “Little Dorrit” of the day with great inward satisfaction.
